key_points: B

options.B: The normal at the point of incidence

key_points: C

questions.text: A ray of light passes from medium 1 (n₁ = 1.5) into medium 2 (n₂ = 1.0). The ray will:

questions.text: State the two laws of reflection of light.

key_points:
1. The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection (∠i = ∠r).
2. The incident ray, the reflected ray, and the normal to the reflecting surface at the point of incidence all lie in the same plane.

questions.text: Define the following terms for a spherical mirror: (i) Pole, (ii) Centre of curvature, (iii) Principal focus.

key_points:
(i) Pole (P): The midpoint of the reflecting surface of a spherical mirror.
(ii) Centre of curvature (C): The centre of the sphere of which the mirror is a part. It lies at a distance R (radius of curvature) from the pole.
(iii) Principal focus (F): The point on the principal axis where rays parallel to the axis converge (concave) or appear to diverge from (convex) after reflection. Distance PF = f (focal length).
rubric.expected_answer:
(i) Pole (P): The midpoint of the reflecting surface of a spherical mirror.
(ii) Centre of curvature (C): The centre of the sphere of which the mirror is a part. It lies at a distance R (radius of curvature) from the pole.
(iii) Principal focus (F): The point on the principal axis where rays parallel to the axis converge (concave) or appear to diverge from (convex) after reflection. Distance PF = f (focal length).

questions.text: State the New Cartesian Sign Convention for spherical mirrors.

key_points:
1. All distances are measured from the pole P of the mirror.
2. Distances measured in the direction of incident light (positive x-axis, i.e., from right to left for a mirror) are positive.
3. Distances measured against the direction of incident light are negative.
4. Heights above the principal axis are positive; heights below are negative.
Consequences: u is always negative (real object); f and R are negative for concave mirrors, positive for convex mirrors.
rubric.expected_answer:
1. All distances are measured from the pole P of the mirror.
2. Distances measured in the direction of incident light (positive x-axis, i.e., from right to left for a mirror) are positive.
3. Distances measured against the direction of incident light are negative.
4. Heights above the principal axis are positive; heights below are negative.
Consequences: u is always negative (real object); f and R are negative for concave mirrors, positive for convex mirrors.

questions.text: An object 5 cm tall is placed 30 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 15 cm. Find the position, size, and nature of the image.

key_points:
Given: u = –30 cm, f = –15 cm, h = +5 cm
Mirror formula: 1/v + 1/u = 1/f
1/v = 1/f – 1/u = 1/(–15) – 1/(–30) = –1/15 + 1/30 = –2/30 + 1/30 = –1/30
∴ v = –30 cm
m = –v/u = –(–30)/(–30) = –1
Image height = m × h = –1 × 5 = –5 cm
Image: 30 cm in front of mirror, same size as object, real and inverted.

questions.text: State Snell's law of refraction. Write its mathematical form.

key_points:
Snell's Law: For a given pair of media, the ratio of the sine of the angle of incidence to the sine of the angle of refraction is constant.

Mathematically: sin i / sin r = n₂₁ (constant = refractive index of medium 2 w.r.t. medium 1)
or: n₁ sin i = n₂ sin r  (general form)
The incident ray, refracted ray, and normal at the point of incidence are coplanar.

questions.text: Distinguish between a convex lens and a concave lens on the basis of: (i) shape, (ii) effect on a parallel beam of light.

key_points:
(i) Shape: A convex (converging) lens is thicker at the centre than at the edges. A concave (diverging) lens is thinner at the centre than at the edges.
(ii) Effect on parallel beam: A convex lens converges (brings together) parallel rays at the principal focus on the other side. A concave lens diverges (spreads out) parallel rays; they appear to come from the principal focus on the same side as the incident light.
rubric.expected_answer:
(i) Shape: A convex (converging) lens is thicker at the centre than at the edges. A concave (diverging) lens is thinner at the centre than at the edges.
(ii) Effect on parallel beam: A convex lens converges (brings together) parallel rays at the principal focus on the other side. A concave lens diverges (spreads out) parallel rays; they appear to come from the principal focus on the same side as the incident light.

∴ v = +30 cm
m = v/u = 30/(–15) = –2
Image is 30 cm on the other side of the lens, real, inverted, and magnified (×2).

questions.text: A convex mirror used for rear-view has a radius of curvature of 3.00 m. If a bus is located 5.00 m from this mirror, find the position and magnification of the image.

questions.text: A ray of light travelling in air enters a glass slab of refractive index 1.5 at an angle of 30° to the normal. Find the angle of refraction inside the glass.

key_points:
Using Snell's law: n₁ sin i = n₂ sin r
1.0 × sin 30° = 1.5 × sin r
0.5 = 1.5 sin r
sin r = 0.5/1.5 = 0.333
r = sin⁻¹(0.333) ≈ 19.5°
The angle of refraction inside the glass is approximately 19.5°.

r = sin⁻¹(0.333) ≈ 19.5°
The angle of refraction inside the glass is approximately 19.5°.

questions.text: Explain why the image formed by a convex mirror is always virtual and erect, irrespective of the position of the object.

key_points:
For a convex mirror f > 0. For a real object u < 0. From the mirror formula: 1/v = 1/f – 1/u = 1/f + 1/|u|. Both terms are positive, so v > 0 always — meaning the image forms behind the mirror → virtual.
Magnification m = –v/u. Since v > 0 and u < 0, m = –(+)/(–) = positive → erect.
Therefore, the image is always virtual and erect, regardless of object position.
rubric.expected_answer:
For a convex mirror f > 0. For a real object u < 0. From the mirror formula: 1/v = 1/f – 1/u = 1/f + 1/|u|. Both terms are positive, so v > 0 always — meaning the image forms behind the mirror → virtual.
Magnification m = –v/u. Since v > 0 and u < 0, m = –(+)/(–) = positive → erect.
Therefore, the image is always virtual and erect, regardless of object position.

All experiments give f ≈ 20 cm → results are consistent. The lens has focal length 20 cm.

4. Solar furnaces — large concave mirrors concentrate sunlight at the focus to generate high temperatures.
5. Satellite dish (parabolic type) — similar principle.

questions.text: A ray of light entering a rectangular glass slab (n = 1.5) at an angle of 45° emerges parallel to the incident ray from the opposite face. (i) Find the angle of refraction at the first face. (ii) Explain why the emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray. (iii) Draw the ray path through the slab.

key_points:
(i) At first face: n₁ sin 45° = n₂ sin r₂
1.0 × (1/√2) = 1.5 × sin r₂
sin r₂ = 0.4714 ⟹ r₂ ≈ 28.1°

(ii) At the second face the geometry is reversed — angle of incidence inside = 28.1°, n changes from 1.5 → 1.0, so emergent angle = 45° again. Since the two refracting surfaces are parallel, the incident and emergent rays are parallel (but laterally displaced).

(iii) Diagram: Show incident ray at 45°, refracted ray inside slab at ~28°, emergent ray at 45° — all three in the same plane, with lateral displacement labelled.

questions.text: Derive the lens formula 1/v – 1/u = 1/f for a convex lens, using a ray diagram. State the sign convention used.

key_points:
Sign convention (NCSC): all distances from optical centre O; distances along incident light direction are positive.

Derivation:
Let object AB be at distance u (negative, real). Rays from B:
• Ray 1: Parallel to axis → refracts through focus F₂ on other side.
• Ray 2: Through optical centre O → passes undeviated.
Image A'B' forms at distance v.

Triangles ABО and A'B'О are similar (by AA):
  A'B'/AB = OA'/OA  ⟹  v/u (with signs)

Triangles OA'B' and OF₂F' are similar:
  A'B'/OF = OA'/OF₂
  ⟹  (–v)/(f) = (–v – (–f))/(–f)   [applying sign convention carefully]

After algebraic manipulation:
  1/v – 1/u = 1/f  ✓

This is the thin lens formula.
rubric.expected_answer:
Sign convention (NCSC): all distances from optical centre O; distances along incident light direction are positive.

Derivation:

• Ray 1: Parallel to axis → refracts through focus F₂ on other side.
• Ray 2: Through optical centre O → passes undeviated.
Image A'B' forms at distance v.

Triangles ABО and A'B'О are similar (by AA):
  A'B'/AB = OA'/OA  ⟹  v/u (with signs)

Triangles OA'B' and OF₂F' are similar:
  A'B'/OF = OA'/OF₂
  ⟹  (–v)/(f) = (–v – (–f))/(–f)   [applying sign convention carefully]

After algebraic manipulation:

This is the thin lens formula.

questions.text: Derive the mirror formula 1/v + 1/u = 1/f for a concave mirror forming a real image of a real object. State the sign convention and the assumptions made.

key_points:
Assumptions: (i) Mirror is small (aperture << R), (ii) object is a point on the principal axis, (iii) paraxial rays only.

Sign convention: Distances measured from pole P; direction of incident light is negative x.

Derivation:
Object AB at distance u (negative) in front of concave mirror (f negative).
Ray from B parallel to axis reflects through F.
Ray through C reflects back on itself.
Image A'B' forms at v (negative for real image).

Triangles ABP and A'B'P are similar:
  A'B'/AB = PA'/PA = v/u

Triangles ABF and FPM (where M is on mirror) are similar:
  A'B'/MP = FA'/FP
  But MP = AB, FA' = PA' – PF = v – f
  ⟹  v/u = (v – f)/f
  ⟹  vf = u(v – f) = uv – uf
  Divide throughout by uvf:
  1/u + 1/v = 1/f  ✓

Relation between f and R: f = R/2.

Assumptions: (i) Mirror is small (aperture << R), (ii) object is a point on the principal axis, (iii) paraxial rays only.

questions.text:
Assertion (A): A concave lens always forms a virtual image for a real object.
Reason (R): The focal length of a concave lens is negative, so the lens formula always gives a negative value of v for a real object.

Choose the correct option:
(a) Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
(b) Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
(c) A is true but R is false.
(d) A is false but R is true.

options.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
options.b: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.
options.c: A is true but R is false.
options.d: A is false but R is true.

key_points: a
rubric.expected_answer:
a
For concave lens f < 0, u < 0 (real object). 1/v = 1/f + 1/u — both terms negative → v < 0 always → virtual image. R correctly explains A.

questions.text: When a ray of light strikes a plane mirror at 90° to the mirror surface, it:

options.B: Reflects back along the same path

key_points: B
rubric.expected_answer:
B
90° to the mirror surface = 0° to the normal. Angle of incidence = 0°, so angle of reflection = 0° — ray returns on itself.

questions.text: The focal length of a concave mirror is 10 cm. Its radius of curvature is:

key_points: C

questions.text: An object placed 10 cm in front of a mirror gives a virtual, erect image twice as large. The mirror is:

key_points: B
rubric.expected_answer:
B
m = +2 (virtual, erect) → –v/u = 2 → v = –2u = +20 cm (behind mirror). u = –10 cm. 1/f = 1/v + 1/u = 1/20 + 1/(–10) = –1/20. f = –20 cm → concave.

questions.text: Light travels from glass (n = 1.5) to water (n = 1.33). The light ray will:

key_points: A
rubric.expected_answer:
A
Glass (denser, n=1.5) to water (less dense, n=1.33): ray bends away from normal.

questions.text: A ray of light falls on the boundary between two media of refractive indices n₁ and n₂ (n₁ < n₂). Total internal reflection will occur when:

options.A: Light travels from medium 1 to medium 2 beyond critical angle
options.B: Light travels from medium 2 to medium 1 beyond critical angle
options.C: Light travels normally to the surface

key_points: B
rubric.expected_answer:
B
TIR occurs when light goes from denser (n₂) to rarer (n₁) medium AND the angle of incidence exceeds the critical angle.

questions.text: An object is placed at the focus of a convex lens. The image formed is:

options.C: At F on same side, virtual

key_points: B
rubric.expected_answer:
B
u = –f. 1/v = 1/f + 1/u = 1/f – 1/f = 0 → v = ∞. Image at infinity, real, highly magnified.

questions.text: Which of the following graphs correctly represents the relationship between image distance (v) and object distance (u) for a convex lens (real image only)?

options.A: A straight line through the origin
options.B: A hyperbola in the second quadrant (u negative, v positive)
options.D: A straight line parallel to the v-axis

key_points: B
rubric.expected_answer:
B
1/v – 1/u = 1/f → 1/v = 1/f + 1/u: for u < –f (real object beyond focus), v is positive and decreases as |u| increases. The locus is a rectangular hyperbola in the quadrant where u < 0 and v > 0.

questions.text: A person uses a lens of power +3.5 D to read a book. The minimum distance from the lens at which the book can be read clearly (near point) is approximately:

key_points: B
rubric.expected_answer:
B
f = 1/P = 1/3.5 = 0.286 m = 28.6 cm. The focal length gives the minimum distance for parallel rays (object at ∞ → image at f). For a reading lens this is approximate.

questions.text: In a concave mirror experiment, when the object distance equals the focal length, the image is at infinity. Which formula confirms this?

options.D: f = R/2 only holds for small apertures

key_points: A
rubric.expected_answer:
A
With u = –f (concave, f negative): 1/v = 1/f – 1/u = 1/f – 1/(–f) = 2/f — wait, recalculate: 1/v = 1/f – 1/u = (–1/|f|) – (–1/|f|) = 0, confirming v → ∞.

questions.text: The phenomenon responsible for the formation of a rainbow is:

key_points: C
rubric.expected_answer:
C
Rainbows form by dispersion (different wavelengths refract at different angles) combined with total internal reflection inside raindrops.

questions.text: The net power of two lenses in contact is zero. This means:

options.B: The lenses have equal focal lengths
options.C: One lens is convex, the other concave with equal magnitude focal lengths
options.D: The combination acts like a concave mirror

key_points: C
rubric.expected_answer:
C
P = P₁ + P₂ = 0 → P₁ = –P₂ → lenses have equal magnitude but opposite sign focal lengths: one convex (+f), one concave (–f).

questions.text: A student states: 'For a real image formed by a concave mirror, magnification is always negative.' Is this correct?

options.A: Yes — real images from concave mirrors are always inverted.
options.B: No — real images can be erect if the object is virtual.
options.C: No — magnification is positive for all real images.
options.D: Yes — but only when the object is beyond C.

key_points: A
rubric.expected_answer:
A
For a concave mirror forming a real image, both u and v are negative (real object, real image in front of mirror), so m = –v/u = –(negative)/(negative) = negative. Real images are always inverted → m < 0. Option A is correct.

questions.text: Why does a concave mirror produce both real and virtual images whereas a convex mirror always produces a virtual image? Explain in terms of ray geometry.

key_points:
Concave mirror: The reflecting surface curves inward — it can converge reflected rays to a real focus (when object is beyond F), or if the object is between P and F, the reflected rays diverge and only appear to meet behind the mirror (virtual image). So the nature of image depends on object position.

Convex mirror: The reflecting surface curves outward — reflected rays always diverge. Extending them behind the mirror gives a virtual focus. For any real object, the reflected rays are always diverging, so the image is always virtual, erect, and diminished behind the mirror.
rubric.expected_answer:
Concave mirror: The reflecting surface curves inward — it can converge reflected rays to a real focus (when object is beyond F), or if the object is between P and F, the reflected rays diverge and only appear to meet behind the mirror (virtual image). So the nature of image depends on object position.

Convex mirror: The reflecting surface curves outward — reflected rays always diverge. Extending them behind the mirror gives a virtual focus. For any real object, the reflected rays are always diverging, so the image is always virtual, erect, and diminished behind the mirror.

questions.text: A coin is placed at the bottom of a container filled with water (n = 1.33) to a depth of 20 cm. What is the apparent depth of the coin as seen from above?

key_points:
Apparent depth = Real depth / n = 20 / 1.33 ≈ 15.0 cm
The coin appears to be only 15 cm below the surface (not 20 cm) due to refraction at the water–air interface.
rubric.expected_answer:
Apparent depth = Real depth / n = 20 / 1.33 ≈ 15.0 cm
The coin appears to be only 15 cm below the surface (not 20 cm) due to refraction at the water–air interface.

questions.text: Draw a ray diagram to show image formation by a convex lens when the object is placed between F and 2F. State the nature, position, and size of the image.

key_points:
Ray diagram: Two rays from tip of object — (1) parallel to axis → passes through F₂ after refraction; (2) through optical centre → undeviated. These rays meet beyond 2F₂ on the other side.

Image: Real, inverted, magnified (|v| > 2f). Positioned beyond 2F₂ on the transmission side.
rubric.expected_answer:
Ray diagram: Two rays from tip of object — (1) parallel to axis → passes through F₂ after refraction; (2) through optical centre → undeviated. These rays meet beyond 2F₂ on the other side.

Image: Real, inverted, magnified (|v| > 2f). Positioned beyond 2F₂ on the transmission side.

questions.text: An optometrist prescribes –3.0 D for a patient's left eye and +1.5 D for the right eye. What is the focal length for each eye? What defects are being corrected?

key_points:
Left eye: f = 1/(–3.0) = –0.333 m = –33.3 cm → concave lens → corrects myopia (short-sightedness).
Right eye: f = 1/(+1.5) = +0.667 m = +66.7 cm → convex lens → corrects hypermetropia (long-sightedness/far-sightedness).
rubric.expected_answer:
Left eye: f = 1/(–3.0) = –0.333 m = –33.3 cm → concave lens → corrects myopia (short-sightedness).
Right eye: f = 1/(+1.5) = +0.667 m = +66.7 cm → convex lens → corrects hypermetropia (long-sightedness/far-sightedness).

questions.text: An object moves from infinity towards a concave mirror of focal length f. Describe qualitatively how the image position and nature change as the object moves from ∞ to the pole P.

key_points:
Object at ∞: image at F (real, inverted, point)
Object beyond C: image between F and C (real, inverted, diminished)
Object at C: image at C (real, inverted, same size as object)
Object between C and F: image beyond C (real, inverted, magnified)
Object at F: image at ∞ (no image formed / image at infinity)
Object between F and P: image behind mirror (virtual, erect, magnified)

Summary: As object approaches from ∞, real image starts at F, moves away, reaches C, then goes to ∞; when object crosses F, image flips to virtual behind mirror and then virtual image also moves to ∞ as object approaches P.
rubric.expected_answer:
Object at ∞: image at F (real, inverted, point)
Object beyond C: image between F and C (real, inverted, diminished)
Object at C: image at C (real, inverted, same size as object)
Object between C and F: image beyond C (real, inverted, magnified)
Object at F: image at ∞ (no image formed / image at infinity)
Object between F and P: image behind mirror (virtual, erect, magnified)

Summary: As object approaches from ∞, real image starts at F, moves away, reaches C, then goes to ∞; when object crosses F, image flips to virtual behind mirror and then virtual image also moves to ∞ as object approaches P.

questions.text: In an experiment to find the focal length of a concave mirror, a student places a bright object and a screen such that a sharp image is formed on the screen. The object distance is 60 cm and the image distance is 60 cm. Calculate the focal length and state at which position of the mirror formula this corresponds.

key_points:
u = –60 cm, v = –60 cm (real image on screen in front of mirror)
1/f = 1/v + 1/u = –1/60 + (–1/60) = –2/60 = –1/30
f = –30 cm
This corresponds to the object at C (u = 2f = –60 cm), giving a real, inverted, same-size image at C.
rubric.expected_answer:
u = –60 cm, v = –60 cm (real image on screen in front of mirror)
1/f = 1/v + 1/u = –1/60 + (–1/60) = –2/60 = –1/30
f = –30 cm
This corresponds to the object at C (u = 2f = –60 cm), giving a real, inverted, same-size image at C.

questions.text: Light of wavelength 600 nm in air enters water (n = 1.33). Find: (i) the speed of light in water, (ii) the wavelength of light in water, (iii) whether the frequency changes.

key_points:
(i) v = c/n = (3×10⁸)/1.33 = 2.26×10⁸ m/s
(ii) λ_water = λ_air/n = 600/1.33 ≈ 451 nm
(iii) Frequency does NOT change (f = c/λ = v/λ_water — both ratios give same f). Frequency is determined by the source and remains constant in all media.
rubric.expected_answer:
(i) v = c/n = (3×10⁸)/1.33 = 2.26×10⁸ m/s
(ii) λ_water = λ_air/n = 600/1.33 ≈ 451 nm
(iii) Frequency does NOT change (f = c/λ = v/λ_water — both ratios give same f). Frequency is determined by the source and remains constant in all media.

questions.text: Compare the image formed by a convex lens for an object placed (i) at 2F and (ii) between F and 2F. Tabulate position, size, nature.

key_points:
| Object position | Image position | Size | Nature |
|---|---|---|---|
| At 2F | At 2F (other side) | Same size | Real, inverted |
| Between F & 2F | Beyond 2F (other side) | Magnified | Real, inverted |

As object moves from 2F towards F, image moves from 2F towards infinity and becomes progressively more magnified.

| Object position | Image position | Size | Nature |
|---|---|---|---|
| At 2F | At 2F (other side) | Same size | Real, inverted |
| Between F & 2F | Beyond 2F (other side) | Magnified | Real, inverted |

As object moves from 2F towards F, image moves from 2F towards infinity and becomes progressively more magnified.

questions.text: The magnification produced by a plane mirror is +1. Explain what this tells us about the image.

key_points:
m = +1 means: (i) |m| = 1 → image is the same size as the object; (ii) m > 0 (positive) → image is virtual and erect.
Therefore the image in a plane mirror is virtual, erect, and of the same size as the object, located as far behind the mirror as the object is in front.
rubric.expected_answer:
m = +1 means: (i) |m| = 1 → image is the same size as the object; (ii) m > 0 (positive) → image is virtual and erect.
Therefore the image in a plane mirror is virtual, erect, and of the same size as the object, located as far behind the mirror as the object is in front.

questions.text: A student claims that a concave lens can form a real image. Justify whether this claim is correct or incorrect.

key_points:
The claim is INCORRECT for a real object.
For a concave lens, f < 0 and u < 0. Lens formula: 1/v = 1/f + 1/u — both terms negative → v < 0 always. Negative v means image on same side as object → virtual image.

A concave lens can theoretically form a real image only if the object is virtual (u > 0), but in standard CBSE Class 10 scope, only real objects are considered. Therefore the claim is incorrect.
rubric.expected_answer:
The claim is INCORRECT for a real object.
For a concave lens, f < 0 and u < 0. Lens formula: 1/v = 1/f + 1/u — both terms negative → v < 0 always. Negative v means image on same side as object → virtual image.

A concave lens can theoretically form a real image only if the object is virtual (u > 0), but in standard CBSE Class 10 scope, only real objects are considered. Therefore the claim is incorrect.

questions.text: Three lenses of powers +5 D, –3 D, and +2 D are placed in contact. Find the equivalent focal length of the combination.

key_points:
P_total = P₁ + P₂ + P₃ = 5 + (–3) + 2 = +4 D
f = 1/P = 1/4 = 0.25 m = +25 cm
The combination acts as a converging lens of focal length 25 cm.
rubric.expected_answer:
P_total = P₁ + P₂ + P₃ = 5 + (–3) + 2 = +4 D
f = 1/P = 1/4 = 0.25 m = +25 cm
The combination acts as a converging lens of focal length 25 cm.

questions.text: A candle flame is placed 30 cm in front of a concave mirror. The image of the flame is formed on a screen placed 30 cm on the other side of the mirror. (i) Is this possible? (ii) Find the focal length. (iii) Describe the image.

key_points:
(i) No — for mirrors, image and object are on the same side (in front). If screen is placed behind the mirror, that is behind the reflecting surface → not physically valid for a standard concave mirror setup.

Corrected interpretation: screen 30 cm in front of mirror on same side:
u = –30 cm, v = –30 cm
1/f = –1/30 + (–1/30) = –2/30 → f = –15 cm
(ii) Focal length = –15 cm (concave, as expected)
(iii) Image is real, inverted, same size as object (object is at C = 2f = 30 cm).
rubric.expected_answer:
(i) No — for mirrors, image and object are on the same side (in front). If screen is placed behind the mirror, that is behind the reflecting surface → not physically valid for a standard concave mirror setup.

Corrected interpretation: screen 30 cm in front of mirror on same side:
u = –30 cm, v = –30 cm
1/f = –1/30 + (–1/30) = –2/30 → f = –15 cm
(ii) Focal length = –15 cm (concave, as expected)
(iii) Image is real, inverted, same size as object (object is at C = 2f = 30 cm).

questions.text: Explain why a pencil appears bent when placed in a glass of water.

key_points: The pencil appears bent because of refraction at the water–air interface. Light from the submerged part of the pencil travels from water (denser, n≈1.33) to air (rarer, n=1.0) and bends away from the normal. Our eye/brain assumes light travels in straight lines, so it extrapolates the rays back and perceives the submerged part at a position different from its actual position — making the pencil appear bent at the interface.

Light from the submerged part of the pencil travels from water (denser, n≈1.33) to air (rarer, n=1.0) and bends away from the normal. Our eye/brain assumes light travels in straight lines, so it extrapolates the rays back and perceives the submerged part at a position different from its actual position — making the pencil appear bent at the interface.

questions.text: A concave mirror has a radius of curvature of 30 cm. An object 2 cm tall is placed 45 cm in front of it. Find: (i) image distance, (ii) image height, (iii) nature of image.

key_points:
f = –R/2 = –15 cm, u = –45 cm, h_o = +2 cm
1/v = 1/f – 1/u = –1/15 – (–1/45) = –3/45 + 1/45 = –2/45
v = –22.5 cm
m = –v/u = –(–22.5)/(–45) = –0.5
h_i = –0.5 × 2 = –1 cm
Image: 22.5 cm in front of mirror, real, inverted, diminished (1 cm tall).
rubric.expected_answer:
f = –R/2 = –15 cm, u = –45 cm, h_o = +2 cm
1/v = 1/f – 1/u = –1/15 – (–1/45) = –3/45 + 1/45 = –2/45
v = –22.5 cm
m = –v/u = –(–22.5)/(–45) = –0.5
h_i = –0.5 × 2 = –1 cm
Image: 22.5 cm in front of mirror, real, inverted, diminished (1 cm tall).

questions.text: An object is placed 25 cm in front of a convex lens of focal length 20 cm. Find image distance, magnification, and state if the image is real or virtual.

key_points:
u = –25 cm, f = +20 cm
1/v = 1/f + 1/u = 1/20 + 1/(–25) = 5/100 – 4/100 = 1/100
v = +100 cm
m = v/u = 100/(–25) = –4
Image is 100 cm on the other side of lens, real, inverted, magnified 4×.
rubric.expected_answer:
u = –25 cm, f = +20 cm
1/v = 1/f + 1/u = 1/20 + 1/(–25) = 5/100 – 4/100 = 1/100
v = +100 cm
m = v/u = 100/(–25) = –4
Image is 100 cm on the other side of lens, real, inverted, magnified 4×.

questions.text: Light travels from glass (n = 1.5) to water (n = 1.33) with an angle of incidence of 40°. Find the angle of refraction. (sin 40° = 0.643)

key_points:
n₁ sin i = n₂ sin r
1.5 × sin 40° = 1.33 × sin r
1.5 × 0.643 = 1.33 × sin r
0.9645 = 1.33 sin r
sin r = 0.9645/1.33 = 0.7252
r = sin⁻¹(0.7252) ≈ 46.5°
The ray bends away from the normal (46.5° > 40°) as it goes from denser glass to less dense water.
rubric.expected_answer:
n₁ sin i = n₂ sin r
1.5 × sin 40° = 1.33 × sin r
1.5 × 0.643 = 1.33 × sin r
0.9645 = 1.33 sin r
sin r = 0.9645/1.33 = 0.7252
r = sin⁻¹(0.7252) ≈ 46.5°
The ray bends away from the normal (46.5° > 40°) as it goes from denser glass to less dense water.

questions.text:
Riya tries to see a coin at the bottom of an empty bowl but cannot see it from her seat. Her friend slowly pours water into the bowl, and the coin becomes visible without Riya moving.

(a) Name the phenomenon responsible for this observation. [1]
(b) In which direction does light bend when it enters water from air? [1]
(c) Draw a labelled ray diagram showing how light from the coin reaches Riya's eye. [2]

key_points: Refraction of light is the phenomenon responsible
Light bends towards the normal when entering denser medium (water)
Ray diagram shows light bending at water-air interface from coin to eye
Correct labelling: incident ray, refracted ray, normal, interface
rubric.expected_answer: (a) Refraction of light. (b) Towards the normal — water is denser than air. (c) Ray diagram showing light from coin bending at water surface towards Riya's eye.

questions.text: The angle of reflection is measured with respect to:

options.text: The normal to the reflecting surface at the point of incidence

key_points: Both angle of incidence and angle of reflection are always measured from the normal to the surface at the point of incidence
rubric.expected_answer: The normal to the reflecting surface at the point of incidence

questions.text: A concave mirror has a radius of curvature of 30 cm. An object is placed 20 cm in front of the mirror. Find the position of the image formed.

key_points: Step 1: R = 30 cm, so f = R/2 = 15 cm; for a concave mirror f is negative, so f = -15 cm
Step 2: Object is in front of mirror, so u = -20 cm (New Cartesian sign convention)
Step 3: Apply mirror formula: 1/v + 1/u = 1/f  →  1/v = 1/f - 1/u
Final: v = -60 cm — negative means real image formed 60 cm in front of the mirror
rubric.expected_answer: v = -60 cm. The image is real, inverted, and formed 60 cm in front of the concave mirror.

questions.text: An object is placed 10 cm in front of a convex mirror of focal length 15 cm. Find the position of the image.

key_points: Step 1: Convex mirror — focal length is positive: f = +15 cm
Step 2: Object in front of mirror: u = -10 cm
Step 4: v = 30/5 = +6 cm
Final: v = +6 cm — positive means virtual image formed 6 cm behind the mirror (virtual, erect, diminished)
rubric.expected_answer: v = +6 cm. The image is virtual, erect, diminished, and formed 6 cm behind the convex mirror.

questions.text: A concave mirror produces a 3 times magnified real image of an object placed 10 cm in front of it. Find the focal length of the mirror.

key_points: Step 1: Real image is inverted, so m = -3 (negative for real, inverted image)
Final: f = -7.5 cm. Negative confirms it is a concave mirror.
rubric.expected_answer: f = -7.5 cm. The focal length of the concave mirror is 7.5 cm.

questions.text: An object 5 cm tall is placed 25 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 20 cm. Find (i) the image distance and (ii) the height of the image.

key_points: Given: h_o = 5 cm, u = -25 cm, f = -20 cm (concave mirror)
Step 2: v = -100 cm (real image, 100 cm in front of mirror)
Step 3: Magnification m = -v/u = -(-100)/(-25) = -4
Step 4: h_i = m x h_o = -4 x 5 = -20 cm
Final: Image is 100 cm in front of mirror; image height = 20 cm (inverted, enlarged 4 times)
rubric.expected_answer: (i) v = -100 cm  (ii) h_i = -20 cm (inverted image, 20 cm tall)

questions.text: The image formed by a concave mirror is real, inverted, and 4 times the size of the object. If the object is 15 cm from the mirror, find the focal length of the mirror.

key_points: Step 1: Real, inverted image => m = -4
Final: f = -60/5 = -12 cm. Negative sign confirms concave mirror.
rubric.expected_answer: f = -12 cm. The focal length of the concave mirror is 12 cm.

questions.text: A convex lens has a focal length of 25 cm. What is its power?

key_points: Step 1: Convert focal length to metres: f = 25 cm = 0.25 m
Step 2: Power P = 1/f (f in metres) = 1/0.25
Final: P = +4 D. Positive power confirms it is a converging (convex) lens.
rubric.expected_answer: P = +4 D

questions.text: A concave lens has a focal length of 2 m. What is its power?

key_points: Step 1: Concave lens is a diverging lens; focal length is negative: f = -2 m
Step 2: Power P = 1/f = 1/(-2)
Final: P = -0.5 D. Negative power confirms it is a diverging (concave) lens.

questions.text: A convex lens forms an image 60 cm from the lens on the other side when an object is placed 20 cm in front of it. Find (i) the focal length and (ii) the power of the lens.

key_points: Given: u = -20 cm, v = +60 cm (image on other side = positive for real image)
Final: f = 15 cm, P = +6.67 D (converging lens)

questions.text: Two thin lenses of power +3.5 D and -2.5 D are placed in contact. Find the power and focal length of the combination.

key_points: Step 1: For lenses in contact, P_total = P1 + P2 = 3.5 + (-2.5) = +1.0 D
Final: The combination has power +1 D and focal length 1 m. It acts as a converging lens.

questions.text: A convex lens of focal length 20 cm forms an image of an object placed 30 cm from the lens. Find the image distance and describe the nature of the image.

key_points: Given: f = +20 cm (convex), u = -30 cm
Step 2: v = +60 cm (positive => image on opposite side = real)
Step 3: m = v/u = 60/(-30) = -2 (inverted and magnified twice)
Final: v = +60 cm; image is real, inverted, and 2x magnified
rubric.expected_answer: v = +60 cm. Image is real, inverted, magnified (2x), formed on the other side of the lens.

questions.text: An object is placed 40 cm from a concave lens of focal length 20 cm. Find the image distance.

key_points: Step 1: Concave lens => f = -20 cm; u = -40 cm
Final: v = -13.3 cm — negative means virtual image on the same side as the object (erect, diminished)
rubric.expected_answer: v = -13.3 cm. Image is virtual, erect, and diminished, formed on the same side as the object.

questions.text: An object is placed at twice the focal length (u = 2f) of a convex lens of focal length 15 cm. Find the image distance and magnification.

key_points: Step 1: u = -2f = -30 cm, f = +15 cm
Step 3: v = +30 cm
Final: v = +30 cm; m = -1. Image is real, inverted, same size as object, formed at 2f on the other side.
rubric.expected_answer: v = +30 cm, m = -1. Image is real, inverted, and the same size as the object.

questions.text: Light travels at 2 x 10^8 m/s in a glass slab. Calculate the refractive index of glass. (Speed of light in vacuum = 3 x 10^8 m/s)

key_points: Step 1: Refractive index n = speed of light in vacuum / speed of light in medium
Final: n = 1.5. This shows glass is optically denser than vacuum/air — light slows down when entering glass.

questions.text: The refractive index of diamond is 2.42. Find the speed of light in diamond. (Speed of light in vacuum = 3 x 10^8 m/s)

key_points: Step 1: n = c/v  =>  rearrange to get v = c/n
Final: v = 1.24 x 10^8 m/s. Diamond has a very high refractive index, so light slows down significantly inside it — this causes the sparkle effect.

questions.text: Which of the following statements correctly describes the first law of reflection?

options.text: The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, measured from the reflecting surface
The incident ray, reflected ray, and normal all lie in the same plane
The angle of incidence is always greater than the angle of reflection
The normal is parallel to the reflecting surface

key_points: The first law of reflection states that the incident ray, the normal at the point of incidence, and the reflected ray all lie in the same plane.
The second law states that the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection (both measured from the normal, not the surface).
rubric.expected_answer: Option B — the incident ray, reflected ray, and normal all lie in the same plane.

questions.text: A ray of light strikes a plane mirror at an angle of 35 degrees to the surface. What is the angle of reflection?

key_points: Angle with the surface = 35 degrees; angle of incidence (from normal) = 90 - 35 = 55 degrees.
By the law of reflection, angle of reflection = angle of incidence = 55 degrees.
rubric.formula: angle of incidence = 90 - angle with surface
rubric.expected_answer: Option B — 55 degrees. The angle from the normal is 90 - 35 = 55 degrees.

questions.text: Which property of light is used in the working of a periscope?

key_points: A periscope uses two plane mirrors inclined at 45 degrees to redirect light around a corner.
Each mirror reflects the incident ray by regular (specular) reflection, obeying the laws of reflection.
rubric.expected_answer: Option C — regular reflection from plane mirrors.

questions.text: What is the difference between regular (specular) reflection and diffuse reflection?

key_points: Regular (specular) reflection occurs from smooth, polished surfaces — parallel incident rays reflect as parallel reflected rays.
Diffuse reflection occurs from rough surfaces — parallel incident rays scatter in many different directions because the surface has many tiny irregularities, each with a different normal.
Both types obey the laws of reflection at each point of incidence.
rubric.expected_answer: Regular reflection (smooth surfaces): parallel rays remain parallel after reflection. Diffuse reflection (rough surfaces): parallel rays scatter in many directions. Both obey laws of reflection at each point.
